Brown Butter Maple Cookies (Bakery Style Fall Favorite)

These brown butter maple cookies are bringing the good stuff! Toasty butter and real maple syrup give each cookie a deep caramel sweetness, while the edges turn lightly golden and the middles stay soft and chewy. This brown butter maple syrup cookie recipe brings all that cozy fall flavor together. Scoop them big for 16 thick cookies, then add a little maple glaze if you want a sweet finish that makes the tops shine.

If you’re riding a full‑on maple wave (honestly, same), you’ll love some of my other maple‑kissed treats — like Maple Peanut Butter Cookies, Soft Maple Brown Sugar Cookies, or Maple Chai Snack Cake that disappears before it even cools. They all match the same cozy, fall‑sweet vibe as these chewy brown butter maple cookies. They’re the kind of bakery style maple cookies everyone reaches for first.

Why You’ll Love These Brown Butter Maple Cookies

Brown butter gives these cookies a toasted, almost butterscotch flavor, and pure maple syrup makes every bite taste like the real thing. This maple syrup cookie recipe is perfect for bakers who love deep, warm flavors. They’re lovely plain, but a thin maple drizzle makes them especially fun for a fall cookie plate!

  • Big 1/4-cup scoops bake into thick chewy brown butter maple cookies with soft middles and golden edges. That’s my kind of bakery cookie! They bake up just like bakery style maple cookies — thick, tall, and beautifully golden.
  • Brown sugar keeps the centers chewy, while a little granulated sugar helps the edges get that delicate finish.
  • You can keep the dough plain or add white chocolate chips, maple chips, or pecans. The maple still gets to be the star.

And yes, the brown butter is worth watching closely. Those little golden bits carry so much flavor! If this is your first batch, my guide to making brown butter shows exactly what to look for in the pan.

Ingredients for Brown Butter Maple Cookies

You’ll need 1 cup of butter, two sugars, eggs, maple syrup, vanilla, flour, baking soda, baking powder, and salt. I like pure maple syrup here because pancake syrup won’t bring the same maple flavor. That’s why this maple syrup cookie recipe relies on the real stuff for the best flavor. Maple extract is optional, but it’s a nice boost if you want that flavor to stand out even after baking.

  • Brown butter: 1 cup unsalted butter, browned with all the tasty golden bits.
  • Sugars: 1 cup packed brown sugar and 1/2 cup granulated sugar.
  • Wet ingredients: 2 large eggs, 2 teaspoons vanilla extract, 1/4 cup pure maple syrup, and 1 teaspoon optional maple extract.
  • Dry ingredients: 3 cups all-purpose flour, 1 teaspoon baking soda, 1/2 teaspoon baking powder, and 1/2 teaspoon salt.
  • Optional mix-ins: Up to 1 1/2 cups white chocolate chips or maple baking chips, 1/2 cup chopped pecans, and 1 teaspoon cinnamon.
  • Optional glaze: 1 cup powdered sugar, 2 to 3 tablespoons pure maple syrup, and a pinch of salt.

Measure the flour by spooning it into your cup and leveling it off. Packing flour into the cup can make a thick cookie dry instead of chewy. Also, choose just one kind of baking chip or skip the chips altogether if you want the brown butter and maple front and center.

How to Make Thick Maple Cookies

Brown the butter, mix the dough, scoop it before chilling, and bake the cold mounds at 350°F. Keep the browned bits when you pour the butter from the pan. They’re the best part! This recipe makes about 16 cookies when each scoop holds 1/4 cup of dough.

  1. Place 1 cup unsalted butter in a light-colored saucepan over medium heat. Stir or swirl often until it foams and the bits on the bottom turn golden brown and smell nutty. Immediately pour the butter and browned bits into a heat-safe mixing bowl. Cool for 10 to 15 minutes so the eggs won’t cook when you add them.
  2. Whisk 1 cup packed brown sugar and 1/2 cup granulated sugar into the cooled brown butter. Whisk in 2 large eggs, 2 teaspoons vanilla extract, 1/4 cup pure maple syrup, and 1 teaspoon maple extract if using.
  3. In a separate bowl, whisk together 3 cups all-purpose flour, 1 teaspoon baking soda, 1/2 teaspoon baking powder, and 1/2 teaspoon salt. If you want cinnamon, add 1 teaspoon now. Stir the dry mixture into the butter mixture just until no flour remains. Fold in up to 1 1/2 cups white chocolate or maple chips and 1/2 cup chopped pecans if using.
  4. Scoop the dough into about 16 tall, 1/4-cup mounds on a parchment-lined sheet. Chill the scooped dough in the refrigerator for 30 to 60 minutes. For a quicker firm-up, freeze the mounds for 20 to 30 minutes instead. Chilling after scooping makes the firm dough much easier to handle. This step is key for achieving bakery style maple cookies with soft centers.
  5. Heat the oven to 350°F. Set 6 cold, 1/4-cup dough mounds on each parchment-lined baking sheet, leaving room between them. Bake one sheet at a time for 10 to 13 minutes, checking for set edges and centers that still look a little soft. If the dough is fully frozen, allow about 1 to 2 extra minutes. Let the cookies rest on the hot sheet for 10 minutes before moving them to a rack.
  6. For the optional glaze, whisk 1 cup powdered sugar with 2 tablespoons pure maple syrup and a pinch of salt. Add up to 1 more tablespoon maple syrup, a little at a time, until the glaze drizzles easily. Spoon it over the fully cooled cookies and let it set before stacking.

For jumbo chewy brown butter maple cookies, use a larger scoop and start checking at 14 minutes; they may take 14 to 17 minutes. That larger scoop changes the yield, so the 16-cookie count applies to the 1/4-cup size. Either way, don’t wait for the centers to look fully firm in the oven. They finish setting on the warm pan.

How to Store Brown Butter Maple Cookies

Store completely cooled cookies in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 4 days. If you’ve added the glaze, let it set first and place parchment between layers so the tops stay pretty. These bakery style maple cookies stay soft and chewy for days. For longer storage, freeze the baked cookies in a sealed container for up to 2 months; thaw them at room temperature.

You can also freeze unbaked 1/4-cup dough mounds. Firm them up on a lined sheet, then transfer them to a freezer bag for up to 2 months. Bake from frozen at 350°F and begin checking about 1 to 2 minutes later than the chilled-dough timing. A warm cookie and a cold glass of milk? Yes, please!

Brown Butter Maple Cookie Variations

For a stronger maple finish, add the optional 1 teaspoon maple extract and glaze the cooled cookies. This variation is perfect if you want a maple syrup cookie recipe with an even bolder maple punch. The glaze is also a sweet way to dress up an otherwise plain batch without crowding the dough.

  • For a little crunch, fold in 1/2 cup chopped pecans. Toast them first if you like a deeper nut flavor.
  • For creamy pockets, add up to 1 1/2 cups white chocolate chips. Maple baking chips work too, though I wouldn’t use both full amounts together.
  • For warm spice, stir 1 teaspoon cinnamon into the flour mixture. It gives the maple a lovely autumn nudge.

Prefer another maple cookie with a peanut butter twist? Try these thick maple peanut butter cookies. And if you’ve got apples to bake, this maple apple pecan bread brings that same maple sweetness to the breakfast table.

If you’re searching for a maple syrup cookie recipe with chewy centers and golden edges, this one checks every box.

Brown Butter Maple Cookie FAQs

Why did my brown butter maple cookies spread?

Warm dough is the most likely reason. Scoop the dough into tall 1/4-cup mounds, then chill it for the full 30 to 60 minutes before baking. Also, let the browned butter cool for 10 to 15 minutes before you mix in the sugars and eggs.

Can I make these maple cookies without maple extract?

Yes. The 1/4 cup pure maple syrup stays in the dough, so the cookies still have maple flavor. The optional 1 teaspoon maple extract makes it more pronounced, especially if you leave off the glaze.

How do I keep thick maple cookies chewy?

Pull them from the 350°F oven when the edges are set but the centers still look slightly soft. Let them sit on the baking sheet for 10 minutes, then move them to a rack. Baking until the centers look dry can take away that lovely chew.

Can I freeze the dough?

Yes. Freeze the scooped 1/4-cup mounds on a lined sheet, then seal them in a freezer bag for up to 2 months. Bake them from frozen at 350°F and add about 1 to 2 minutes to the 10 to 13 minute bake window.

Let’s Bake a Batch!

Brown the butter until it’s nutty, scoop that maple dough nice and tall, and get ready for thick, chewy cookies with golden edges! Leave them plain to taste every bit of the toasted butter or add a shiny maple drizzle. These truly bake up like bakery style maple cookies — thick, tall, and full of maple‑brown‑butter goodness. Then show me your batch on Instagram, save the recipe on Pinterest, and share your cookie plate on Facebook. Happy baking!

Brown Butter Maple Cookies

Kim Lange
Thick, chewy brown butter maple cookies with golden edges, soft centers, and an optional maple glaze. Makes about 16 cookies using 1/4 cup dough each.
No ratings yet
Print Recipe Pin Recipe
Prep Time 20 minutes mins
Cook Time 13 minutes mins
Chill Time 30 minutes mins
Total Time 1 hour hr 3 minutes mins
Course Dessert
Cuisine American
Servings 16 cookies
Calories 436 kcal

Equipment

  • Light-colored saucepan
  • Heat-safe mixing bowl
  • Mixing bowl
  • Whisk
  • Rubber spatula
  • 1/4-cup measuring cup or cookie scoop
  • Baking sheets
  • Parchment paper
  • Wire cooling rack

Ingredients
  

Brown Butter

  • 1 cup unsalted butter

Cookie Dough

  • 1 cup packed brown sugar
  • ½ cup granulated sugar
  • 2 large eggs
  • 2 teaspoons vanilla extract
  • ¼ cup pure maple syrup
  • 1 teaspoon maple extract optional
  • 3 cups all-purpose flour spooned and leveled
  • 1 teaspoon baking soda
  • ½ teaspoon baking powder
  • ½ teaspoon salt
  • 1 ½ cups white chocolate chips or maple baking chips optional
  • ½ cup chopped pecans optional
  • 1 teaspoon ground cinnamon optional

Optional Maple Glaze

  • 1 cup powdered sugar
  • 2 to 3 tablespoons pure maple syrup
  • 1 pinch salt

Instructions
 

Brown the Butter

  • Brown 1 cup unsalted butter in a light-colored saucepan over medium heat, stirring or swirling often until the butter smells nutty and the milk solids turn golden brown. Pour the butter and browned bits into a heat-safe bowl and cool for 10 to 15 minutes.

Mix the Dough

  • Whisk 1 cup packed brown sugar and 1/2 cup granulated sugar into the cooled brown butter. Whisk in 2 large eggs, 2 teaspoons vanilla extract, 1/4 cup pure maple syrup, and 1 teaspoon maple extract if using.
  • Whisk 3 cups all-purpose flour, 1 teaspoon baking soda, 1/2 teaspoon baking powder, 1/2 teaspoon salt, and 1 teaspoon optional cinnamon in a separate bowl. Stir the dry mixture into the wet mixture just until combined. Fold in up to 1 1/2 cups optional white chocolate or maple chips and 1/2 cup optional chopped pecans.

Shape, Chill, and Bake

  • Scoop about 16 tall mounds using 1/4 cup dough for each cookie. Chill the mounds on a parchment-lined sheet for 30 to 60 minutes, or flash-freeze them for 20 to 30 minutes.
  • Preheat the oven to 350°F. Space 6 cold, 1/4-cup mounds on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Bake one sheet at a time for 10 to 13 minutes, until the edges are set and the centers still look slightly soft. For fully frozen dough, add about 1 to 2 minutes. Cool the cookies on the sheet for 10 minutes, then transfer to a wire rack.

Optional Maple Glaze

  • Whisk 1 cup powdered sugar, 2 tablespoons pure maple syrup, and a pinch of salt. Add up to 1 more tablespoon maple syrup until the glaze drizzles easily. Drizzle over fully cooled cookies and let set.

Notes

  • Use pure maple syrup rather than pancake syrup.
  • Keep the browned milk solids when transferring the butter.
  • The 16-cookie yield and 10- to 13-minute bake time are for 1/4-cup portions. Larger jumbo portions may take 14 to 17 minutes and will reduce the yield.
  • Store baked cookies airtight at room temperature for up to 4 days or freeze for up to 2 months. Freeze scooped dough mounds for up to 2 months and bake from frozen, adding about 1 to 2 minutes.
Nutrition is estimated per 1/4-cup cookie without optional mix-ins or glaze. Actual values vary with ingredient brands and portion size.
